title: KS3 SATs: Should They Be Brought Back?
author: Joel Kenyon
summary: Prompted by a Twitter poll in which 40% of respondents wanted England's abandoned KS3 assessments back, science teacher Joel Kenyon thinks aloud about whether they should return. He first lays out the case against: workload and top-down pressure on teachers and middle leaders, a flood of data and tracking admin, the fact that the results carry no currency with colleges or employers, and a cost that could double the roughly 300 million pounds spent on GCSEs. Then he makes the case for, using primary science as his example: when science left the KS2 assessments, schools gave it less weight, and Year 7 pupils arrive knowing little. He argues exams would align KS3 curricula across schools, make clear what belongs at KS3 versus GCSE, lower the stakes compared with GCSE, and give pupils evidence of what they can achieve before choices at 14. He concludes, tentatively and after only a few hours of writing, that the exams should return, because without them he cannot see how KS3 rigour improves evenly across the country.
points: The strongest objections are practical: extra workload, tracking-data overload for middle leaders, and doubled exam costs with no new funding.
KS3 results carry no external currency, which is why they were scrapped in 2008 and why critics call them redundant.
Kenyon's main argument is alignment: common assessments would give every school the same picture of what, and to what standard, to teach at 11 to 14.
The removal of science from KS2 tests shows how assessment shapes where primary schools put their effort.
Brought back lower-stakes and without the old burdensome teacher assessment, exams might make KS3 a stage with its own rigour rather than a waiting room for GCSE.
quotes: Earlier this week, I posed the question on Twitter of whether we should bring back the KS3 assessments that were abandoned in 2008. The results were interesting in that I had a lot more people saying they would bring them back than I thought I would.
The idea of this pressure on teachers and middle leaders of both Year 9 and Year 11 students does make me wince and would probably be the biggest reason why I would suggest they don’t come back.

If colleges and employers cared more about the GCSEs that sit two later, then what is the actual benefit to the pupil? I will be discussing this later, but again, the redundancy of the exams is a good argument for keeping them scrapped.

Now, I do teach a core subject and I am aware that if KS3 SATs come back, there s a high likelihood that Science would be included. If we look specifically at the KS2 assessments, I think it was wrong to take science out of assessments and my rationale is sometimes one that a lot of science teachers share.

If science was brought back into the KS2 set of exams, there would be a major focus on this, curricula would be aligned and there would be an improvement in knowledge of pupils as they transition to secondary school.

To start with, I do not like the idea of choosing your future at 14 years old and I, as well as many others, have discussed this previously. But with the introduction of the KS3 assessments, it highlights what pathways that would be open to these students at this age.

Schools up and down the country would know exactly what they should be teaching it as well as to what standard. They do need to know the structure of an atom, but you can leave electronic configuration until GCSE because it isn’t assessed until then.
